references.text: The Jews also ask Jesus for a sign here: 'What sign do you perform, so that we may see it and believe you?' (John 6:30). It is a recurring pattern that the Jewish leaders demand signs as proof of Jesus' authority.
The scribes and Pharisees ask Jesus for a sign: 'Teacher, we want to see a sign from you' (Matthew 12:38). Here too, Jesus is challenged to prove his authority through a visible sign.

The Pharisees and Sadducees demand a sign from heaven to test Jesus (Matthew 16:1-4). Jesus answers that this generation will only receive the sign of Jonah, similarly to how he points to his resurrection in John 2:19.
The Pharisees ask Jesus for a sign from heaven to test him (Mark 8:11-12). Jesus sighs deeply and says that this generation will not be given any sign.
Others demanded a sign from heaven from Jesus to test him (Luke 11:16). The demand for signs as proof of divine authority is a recurring theme.
Paul writes that 'Jews demand signs' (1 Corinthians 1:22). This confirms the pattern we see in the Gospels, where Jews continually ask for visible signs as confirmation of a divine mission.

When Moses was sent by God, he received signs to show as proof of his divine authority (Exodus 4:1-9). The Jewish demand for signs in John 2:18 has its background in this tradition that God's messengers confirm their authority with signs.

The cleansing of the temple in John 2:14-16 is the direct occasion for the Jews' demand for a sign. They ask 'because you do these things' (ὅτι ταῦτα ποιεῖς), referring to Jesus' powerful action in the temple.
Jesus had already performed his first sign at Cana (John 2:11). Despite this, the Jews now demand an additional sign to legitimize his authority to cleanse the temple.
Jesus says: 'Unless you see signs and wonders, you will not believe' (John 4:48). This shows Jesus' critical attitude toward a faith that is based solely on the demand for visible signs.
